entries.title: How can a lake make extra snow?
entries.answer: Cold air blowing over a stretch of unfrozen lake picks up heat and water vapor from the water. The warmed, moister air rises and cools. Some of its water forms clouds and then snow. Winds usually carry the clouds toward the far shore of the lake. A narrow area can get much more snow than another place a short drive away, depending on where the wind carries the cloud bands.
facts: Lake-effect snow happens near the Great Lakes and can happen near some other lakes too.

entries.title: How can a snowflake turn into an ice pellet?
entries.answer: Snow may start falling through air cold enough to keep it frozen. Sometimes a layer of warmer air farther down partly melts the flakes. If they then fall through a deep enough layer of below-freezing air close to the ground, they freeze again. They reach the ground as ice pellets. Those pellets may bounce when they hit a hard surface, in contrast to a snowflake that lands softly or a raindrop that splashes.
facts: In weather reports in the United States, sleet means ice pellets.

entries.title: How can invisible air press on things?
entries.answer: Air is made of moving molecules that bump into your skin and other surfaces all the time. Those tiny pushes add up to air pressure. Near sea level, a lot of air lies above you, pressing down on the air below. At the top of a tall mountain, less air rests above you. The pressure is generally lower there. When air pressure changes from place to place, air can start moving as wind.
facts: A barometer is an instrument that measures air pressure.

entries.title: How clouds form
entries.answer: A cloud is a group of very small water drops, ice crystals, or both. Air can carry water as an invisible gas called water vapor. When moist air rises and cools enough, some of the vapor can turn into tiny drops. They often form around very small specks floating in the air. At colder temperatures, ice crystals can form too. A cloud becomes visible because these drops and crystals scatter sunlight. Some clouds form right at ground level. We call those clouds fog.
facts: Water vapor itself is invisible.
You can have a cloud without rain reaching the ground.

entries.title: How do ice crystals grow on a window?
entries.answer: Frost can form when moist air touches a surface that is cold enough for water to turn directly from vapor into ice. The new ice can grow in delicate branches across a window or along a blade of grass. An object outdoors may cool below freezing even if the air a few feet above it is a little warmer. Frost is different from a layer left by rain that lands and then freezes.
facts: A thin frost can form without snow or frozen rain.

entries.title: How does a summer thunderstorm make ice?
entries.answer: A thunderstorm can send a strong stream of air upward. Water droplets often stay liquid even when they are below their usual freezing temperature. When some strike a piece of ice, they can freeze onto it. The growing lump gets heavier as it picks up more. A hailstone falls when the rising air can no longer keep it up or when the wind carries it out into air that is not rising as quickly.
facts: A hailstone can show several layers of ice.

entries.title: How hurricanes get their strength
entries.answer: A hurricane is a large spinning storm that grows over warm ocean water. Warm, moist air rises from the sea. As it cools, water in the air forms clouds and gives off heat. That heat helps fuel more rising air and thunderstorms. The storm can pull in more moist air and keep growing. In a strong hurricane, the clouds may spin around a calmer center called the eye. A hurricane usually weakens after moving over land or much cooler water because it loses its supply of warm, moist ocean air.
facts: A hurricane has steady winds of at least 74 miles per hour.
Some regions call the same kind of storm a typhoon.

entries.title: How rainbows form
entries.answer: A rainbow can appear when sunlight shines into water drops in the air. The light bends on its way into a drop, bounces off the inside, and bends again as it leaves. The different colors bend by different amounts. Light reaching your eyes from some drops looks red, while light from drops at other angles looks blue or violet. Together these views make a colored arc. You can often find a rainbow by looking toward the rain when the Sun is behind you.
facts: A rainbow can be circular, although the ground often blocks the lower part from view.
A rainbow may appear in spray, even when it is not raining.

How does light help us see the bright part of the Moon?

entries.title: Is ground fog really a cloud?
entries.answer: Fog is a cloud close enough to the ground for people to walk through it. On a quiet, clear night, the ground can lose heat. Air touching it cools too. When the air cools enough, some of its invisible water vapor forms tiny liquid drops. Many suspended drops make it harder to see through the air. After sunlight warms the ground and the air again, the drops may evaporate and the fog can thin out.
facts: Fog droplets usually stay in the air rather than falling like rain.

entries.title: Is sea ice made from seawater?
entries.answer: Sea ice starts when ocean water becomes cold enough to freeze. Salt makes seawater freeze at a lower temperature than fresh water. As ice forms, much of the salt stays in the water below or gets trapped in small pockets. Winds and currents can pile pieces together or push them apart. A very different kind of floating ice arrives when part of a glacier breaks off the land and drifts away as an iceberg.
facts: Sea ice comes from the ocean surface freezing.
Most floating ice reflects more sunlight than dark open water does.

entries.title: The water cycle
entries.answer: The same water can be in the ocean one day and in a cloud another day. Some water at the ocean’s surface changes into a gas and mixes with the air. This is evaporation. As moist air cools, some of that gas turns back into tiny drops, forming clouds. When drops or ice crystals grow big enough, they can fall as rain or snow. Water may then soak into the ground, flow down a river, or stay frozen in ice for a long time. The water cycle follows all these paths, and has no single starting point.
facts: Sunlight supplies much of the energy for evaporation.
Some water that falls on land returns to the ocean in rivers.

quiz.question: What is it called when liquid water becomes water vapor?
quiz.explanation: Evaporation happens when some molecules escape from liquid water into the air as a gas.

entries.title: Weather and climate are different
entries.answer: Weather is what the air outside is like now or over a short stretch of time. It might be windy this morning and sunny this afternoon. Climate is the usual pattern of weather in a place over many years. If a place often has hot summers and little rain, those are parts of its climate. A cool or rainy day can still happen there. Scientists use records from many seasons and many years to work out what is common and whether those patterns are changing.
facts: Weather can change within a few minutes.
Scientists often use a 30-year period to describe a place’s usual weather.

entries.title: What a tornado is
entries.answer: A tornado is a fast-spinning column of air that reaches from a storm to the ground. Tornadoes sometimes grow from large thunderstorms that are already turning. Not all of those storms make tornadoes, and scientists are still working out why some do. You may see a funnel when tiny water drops form inside the spinning air. Dust and leaves can show where it touches down. A swirling funnel that stays above the ground is different from a tornado, even if the two look alike from far away.
facts: A tornado can touch the ground even if its visible funnel does not seem to reach all the way down.
A tornado is much smaller than a hurricane.

entries.title: What can you tell from the shape of a cloud?
entries.answer: Gray clouds that spread like a blanket are often stratus clouds. Cumulus clouds can grow in white heaps as air rises in separate columns. Cirrus clouds are usually high, cold, and thin, with streaks that look like wisps of hair. A cloud’s height and shape give clues about the air where it grew. Those clues become more useful when you look at many clouds moving and changing instead of just one cloud for a moment.
facts: Many high cirrus clouds are made mainly of ice crystals.

entries.title: What happens when two kinds of air meet?
entries.answer: A weather front is where a mass of colder air and a mass of warmer air meet. In a cold front, advancing cold air often slides under warm air, which can make the warm air rise quickly. In a warm front, advancing warm air can glide up over colder air close to the ground. Rising air usually cools, allowing clouds and sometimes precipitation to form. If the meeting place barely moves, the weather may linger.
facts: Fronts may bring changes in wind, temperature, and sky cover.

entries.title: What is the jet stream?
entries.answer: High above the ground, there are narrow bands of fast wind called jet streams. They often form near places where there is a large difference in temperature between masses of air. The bands bend and take different routes as the air moves. When jets shift, they can steer some storms along new paths. Airplanes can gain time when they fly in the same direction as a jet stream, because the moving air helps carry them.
facts: Earth has more than one jet stream.

entries.title: What makes lightning and thunder
entries.answer: Inside a storm cloud, bits of ice can bump into each other and help separate electric charges. As the charges build up, electricity can suddenly move through the air. That flash is lightning. It can happen inside a cloud, between clouds, or between a cloud and the ground. Lightning heats the air along its path very fast. The air swells outward, sending out a sound wave that we hear as thunder. We usually see the flash first because light reaches us much faster than sound.
facts: You can see distant lightning even when you cannot hear its thunder.
Lightning flashes can happen without touching the ground.

entries.title: What makes the wind blow?
entries.answer: Air pushes on things even when it looks empty. When air pushes more strongly in one place than in a nearby place, it starts moving from the higher pressure toward lower pressure. Uneven warming of the land and sea can help make pressure differences. Once air moves, the spin of Earth can bend its path over large distances. Buildings, hills, and trees can slow wind or change its direction close to the ground.
facts: A stronger difference in pressure over a short distance can produce stronger wind.

entries.title: Why can falling rain turn to ice on a branch?
entries.answer: Freezing rain begins with liquid drops. Those drops can cool below water’s usual freezing point without turning solid right away. If they reach a surface that is at or below freezing, such as a road or a wire, they can freeze when they land. Drop after drop leaves a coating of ice. Sleet forms in a different way because the drops freeze into pellets before striking anything on the ground.
facts: A clear layer of ice can be hard to see.

questions.text: How do drops that freeze while still falling behave when they land?

entries.title: Why do snowflakes usually have six sides?
entries.answer: A snowflake begins when water forms a tiny ice crystal in a cold cloud. Water molecules fit together in a repeating pattern in ice. The pattern usually gives this kind of crystal six sides or six main branches. As the crystal drifts through the cloud, it can grow new parts. The air’s temperature and moisture affect how it grows. Some crystals look like stars, while others look more like plates, needles, or short columns.
facts: Snow can include crystals stuck together.

entries.title: Why is grass wet on a morning when it did not rain?
entries.answer: After sunset, a blade of grass can cool more quickly than the air a little above it. Air touching the blade also cools. If it cools enough, some of the water vapor in that air turns into tiny liquid drops on the grass. That water is dew. Dew can also appear on a car, a spider web, or a picnic table. A glass of cold water can gain drops on the outside by the same general process.
facts: Dew forms at a surface, while fog droplets hang in the air.

entries.title: Why is most of an iceberg under water?
entries.answer: Icebergs form when pieces break off a glacier or a floating extension of one. An iceberg’s ice is usually made from snow that fell on land, so it is mostly fresh water. Ice is less dense than the water it floats in. Even so, most of a floating iceberg sits underwater, with a smaller share showing above the surface. The hidden part can stretch well beyond the edges a person sees from a boat.
facts: Breaking off blocks of ice at the edge of glaciers is called calving.
